task_3.title: Add attrs field alias support
task_3.description: attrs 22.2.0 adds explicit field aliases so applications can control the keyword names exposed by generated initializers, especially for private attributes, and keeps field introspection and attr.evolve aligned with those effective constructor names.

synthesized_requirement.problem_statement: Ensure that attrs users can explicitly control the generated constructor keyword for each field, including private attributes, and that object construction, field introspection, and evolve-style copying all use the same effective field names.

expectation.grounded: `attr.ib()` and `attrs.field()` should accept an optional `alias` parameter that defines the generated `__init__` argument name for that field. `attr.fields()` and `attr.fields_dict()` should expose the effective constructor name on `Attribute.alias`, using the explicit alias when provided and otherwise the default init name derived from the attribute name. `attr.evolve()` should accept update keywords using the same alias names that the generated initializer accepts, including for underscore-prefixed attributes.
expectation.conceptual: Users should be able to choose the public constructor keyword for an attrs field without changing the stored attribute name. The same name that works during object creation should also be visible through introspection and should be accepted when creating updated copies.

constraints.grounded: Classes that do not specify `alias` should preserve existing constructor behavior, including attrs' current private-attribute init naming rules. Alias handling should remain additive rather than forcing attribute renames, and alias-based construction and evolution should apply through the normal init-enabled field flow. Field transformer usage should remain compatible whether it relies on the default alias or supplies an explicit one.
constraints.conceptual: The new alias capability must be non-breaking for existing callers who do not opt into it. It should preserve current defaults while adding a consistent way to override externally visible constructor names.

behavior: `attr.ib(alias=...)` and `attrs.field(alias=...)` allow a field to expose a custom keyword name in the generated initializer.
For fields without an explicit alias, the effective constructor keyword continues to follow attrs' existing default naming behavior, including underscore stripping for private attribute names.
`attr.fields()` and `attr.fields_dict()` expose each field's effective constructor keyword through `Attribute.alias` for both explicit and default aliases.
`attr.evolve()` resolves change keywords through the field alias mapping so it accepts the same names as the generated initializer for aliased and private fields.
acceptance_criteria: When an attrs class defines a field with `alias`, constructing the class with that alias as the keyword should populate the original attribute on the instance.

When an attrs class defines a private field without an explicit alias, its generated initializer should continue to accept the default keyword name derived by attrs' existing private-name handling, and `Attribute.alias` should report that effective name.
When `attr.fields()` or `attr.fields_dict()` is used on a class that mixes aliased and non-aliased fields, each returned `Attribute` should expose the effective constructor keyword via `.alias`.

When `attr.evolve()` is called on an instance whose fields use custom aliases or default private-field constructor names, it should accept those constructor keywords and return an updated instance without requiring callers to use the stored attribute names.

task_1.title: Drop Python 3.5 support and standardize on Python 3.6+ behavior
task_1.description: attrs 22.2.0 removes Python 3.5 support, treats Python 3.6 as the minimum supported runtime, and aligns public behavior with Python 3.6+ semantics such as ordered standard dictionaries. The upgrade also keeps Python 3.6 working for now but surfaces a deprecation warning for its future removal.

synthesized_requirement.problem_statement: Ensure that upgrading to attrs 22.2.0 is handled as a runtime-compatibility change: Python 3.5 must no longer be treated as supported, Python 3.6+ behavior must rely on normal ordered `dict` semantics, and the public `attr` API must remain consistent for supported runtimes.

expectation.grounded: attrs 22.2.0 must require Python 3.6 or newer. On Python 3.6, importing `attr` should still succeed but emit a `DeprecationWarning` indicating that Python 3.6 support is planned for removal. `attr.fields_dict()` should return a standard `dict` keyed by attribute name in attribute order. When a standard `dict` is passed to `@attr.s(these=...)` or `attr.make_class()`, attribute order should follow that mapping's insertion order, including order-sensitive observable outputs such as generated `repr`. The public names `define`, `field`, `frozen`, and `mutable` should be importable directly from `attr` on supported runtimes.
expectation.conceptual: The library should now be treated as Python-3.6+-only. Supported runtimes should expose one consistent attribute-ordering model based on normal dictionary insertion order, preserve that order in user-visible metadata and representations, and continue exposing the modern top-level `attr` APIs. Python 3.6 remains usable in this release but should warn that it is nearing end of support.

constraints.grounded: Do not require ordered-dictionary-specific types to preserve field order on supported runtimes. Preserve declared or supplied attribute order in public metadata and generated representations. Unsupported Python 3.5 environments should not be considered compatible targets for this release.
constraints.conceptual: Users should not need special container types or version-specific workarounds to get stable field ordering on supported Python versions. The upgrade must keep observable ordering behavior intact while clearly ending compatibility with Python 3.5.

behavior: The package declares Python 3.6 as its minimum supported version and drops Python 3.5 support.
Importing `attr` on Python 3.6 emits a `DeprecationWarning` about planned removal of Python 3.6 support.
`attr.fields_dict()` returns a regular `dict` whose keys and values follow attribute definition order.
A regular `dict` passed to `@attr.s(these=...)` or `attr.make_class()` determines attribute order by insertion order.
Order-sensitive outputs derived from attribute order, including generated `repr`, reflect the insertion order supplied through supported mappings.
The names `define`, `field`, `frozen`, and `mutable` are exported from `attr` for supported runtimes.
acceptance_criteria: When upgrading to attrs 22.2.0, the library should only be considered supported on Python 3.6 or newer.
When `attr` is imported on Python 3.6, it should load successfully and emit a `DeprecationWarning`.
When `attr.fields_dict(SomeAttrsClass)` is called, it should return a `dict` keyed by field name in declared field order.
When a user defines attributes with `@attr.s(these=...)` or `attr.make_class()` using a normal `dict`, the resulting class should preserve that mapping's insertion order for its fields.
When field order affects observable output, such as `repr`, it should match the preserved attribute order.
When importing from `attr` on a supported runtime, `define`, `field`, `frozen`, and `mutable` should be available as top-level names.

task_2.title: Deprecate Python 3.6 in attrs 22.2.0
task_2.description: attrs 22.2.0 formally deprecates Python 3.6. Importing the library on Python 3.6 should continue to work for now, but it must surface a deprecation warning so users know support is planned to be removed in the next release.

synthesized_requirement.problem_statement: Ensure that attrs 22.2.0 explicitly warns users that Python 3.6 is deprecated and will lose support in the next release, while keeping current imports usable during the deprecation window.

expectation.grounded: When `attr` is imported on Python versions earlier than 3.7, package initialization should emit a `DeprecationWarning` about Python 3.6 deprecation and planned removal in the next release, but the import should still succeed. On supported Python versions, this warning should not be emitted. The 22.2.0 top-level `attr` API should remain available after initialization, including `define`, `field`, `frozen`, and `mutable`.
expectation.conceptual: Users running the library on Python 3.6 should be clearly notified that the runtime is nearing end of support without having their current usage break immediately. Users on supported Python versions should see no new warning behavior.

constraints.grounded: The deprecation signal must be a warning rather than an import error or immediate removal of functionality. The warning condition is tied to Python versions below 3.7, and normal package import behavior should remain intact across supported versions.
constraints.conceptual: The update should provide advance notice of upcoming support removal without creating a breaking change in this release, and it should avoid affecting users on still-supported runtimes.

behavior: Importing `attr` on Python 3.6 emits a `DeprecationWarning` during package initialization.
The deprecation warning announces that Python 3.6 support is deprecated in 22.2.0 and intended for removal in the next release.
Importing `attr` on Python 3.6 still completes successfully after the warning is emitted.
Importing `attr` on Python 3.7 or newer does not emit this deprecation warning.
After initialization in 22.2.0, the top-level `attr` namespace exposes `define`, `field`, `frozen`, and `mutable`.
acceptance_criteria: When a consumer imports `attr` on Python 3.6 with warnings captured, it should emit a `DeprecationWarning` indicating that Python 3.6 support is deprecated and scheduled for removal in the next release.
When a consumer imports `attr` on Python 3.6, the module should still load successfully and remain usable after the warning.
When a consumer imports `attr` on Python 3.7 or newer, it should not emit the Python 3.6 deprecation warning.
When a consumer accesses the top-level `attr` API in 22.2.0, `define`, `field`, `frozen`, and `mutable` should be importable from that namespace.

task_4.title: Adopt enum-backed attrs.NOTHING sentinel
task_4.description: The library update changes `attrs.NOTHING` from a custom singleton sentinel to an enum-backed sentinel value so downstream users can reference it in typing constructs such as `typing.Literal`, while preserving its role as the public "no value" marker distinct from `None`.

synthesized_requirement.problem_statement: Ensure that upgrading to attrs 22.2.0 exposes `attrs.NOTHING` as an enum-backed public sentinel that remains usable as the absence marker distinct from `None`, while also allowing downstream typing use cases such as `Literal[NOTHING]`.

expectation.grounded: `attrs.NOTHING` should be a public enum value rather than a custom singleton object. It must remain the sentinel used to represent the lack of a value when `None` is ambiguous, stay falsey in boolean contexts, and preserve its recognizable sentinel representation. The updated form should support downstream type annotations that rely on `typing.Literal[NOTHING]`.
expectation.conceptual: After the upgrade, applications and extensions should continue to treat `attrs.NOTHING` as the library's distinct "no value" marker, but it should now also behave like a typed constant that can be referenced precisely in type annotations.

constraints.grounded: Do not change the public meaning of `attrs.NOTHING` as a sentinel distinct from `None`. Existing runtime behavior that depends on it being falsey or consistently identifiable as the sentinel should continue to work after the enum-based change.
constraints.conceptual: The upgrade should add typing precision without changing what the sentinel means in normal application code or breaking common checks that rely on its established sentinel behavior.

behavior: `attrs.NOTHING` is exposed as an enum member instead of a custom singleton instance.
`attrs.NOTHING` remains the public sentinel for "no value" in cases where `None` would be ambiguous.
`attrs.NOTHING` remains false when evaluated in boolean contexts.
`attrs.NOTHING` keeps a stable, recognizable sentinel representation for user-facing introspection and logging.
Downstream users can reference `attrs.NOTHING` in precise type annotations such as `typing.Literal[NOTHING]`.
acceptance_criteria: When code imports and inspects `attrs.NOTHING`, it should receive a single public sentinel value that is distinct from `None` and backed by an enum member.
When `attrs.NOTHING` is used in a boolean condition, it should evaluate as false.
When developers use `typing.Literal[NOTHING]` in downstream typing for the public sentinel, the upgrade should support that usage.
When application code uses `attrs.NOTHING` to represent an omitted value, its observable sentinel meaning should remain unchanged after the upgrade.
When `attrs.NOTHING` is rendered for debugging or introspection, it should still appear as the established sentinel rather than an opaque internal object.

task_5.title: Restore AttrsInstance on the attrs top-level namespace
task_5.description: attrs 22.2.0 restores the missing AttrsInstance re-export on the top-level attrs package so consumers can rely on attrs.AttrsInstance again. This fixes a 22.1.0 regression that broke typing-oriented usage of the public attrs namespace and made attrs-based type analysis inconsistent in code paths that check attr.has() before calling attr.asdict().

synthesized_requirement.problem_statement: Ensure that upgrading to attrs 22.2.0 restores `AttrsInstance` as a supported top-level symbol on `attrs`, so users do not encounter regressions when referencing `attrs.AttrsInstance` in typed code or attrs-aware object handling.

expectation.grounded: The `attrs` package should publicly expose `AttrsInstance` from its top-level namespace, and that symbol should be included in the package's exported public API. Consumers should be able to resolve `attrs.AttrsInstance` directly, restoring compatibility for static-analysis scenarios that depend on the attrs instance marker while using APIs such as `attr.has()` and `attr.asdict()`.
expectation.conceptual: The main `attrs` import should again provide the attrs instance marker that users and type checkers expect. After the upgrade, code that relies on the public `attrs` namespace for attrs-specific typing should behave consistently instead of failing because the marker is missing.

constraints.grounded: This change should be additive and limited to restoring the missing public export. It should not change the observable behavior of `attr.has()`, `attr.asdict()`, or handling of objects that are not attrs instances, aside from making `AttrsInstance` available through `attrs` again.
constraints.conceptual: The fix should restore the missing public symbol without changing existing attrs detection or serialization semantics. Existing consumers should see a compatibility restoration, not a broader behavioral shift.

behavior: `attrs.AttrsInstance` is available again as a top-level public attribute of the `attrs` package.
`AttrsInstance` is part of the `attrs` public export set, so public-import and API-discovery patterns can see it.
Typed code that depends on resolving the attrs instance marker from the `attrs` namespace no longer breaks because that symbol is missing.
acceptance_criteria: When a consumer imports `attrs`, it should be able to access `attrs.AttrsInstance` as a public symbol.
When a consumer relies on the package's public export surface, `AttrsInstance` should be included alongside the other exported `attrs` names.

When typed application code uses attrs-aware guards such as `attr.has()` before calling `attr.asdict()`, static analysis should be able to resolve the attrs instance marker from the public `attrs` namespace instead of failing due to a missing export.

task_6.title: Restore attrs initializer performance in 22.2.0
task_6.description: attrs 22.2.0 removes the initialization slowdown introduced in 22.1.0 for classes whose generated constructors must bypass custom __setattr__ handling, especially as more attributes are assigned, while preserving the same externally visible initialization and hash-caching behavior.

synthesized_requirement.problem_statement: Ensure that upgrading to attrs 22.2.0 removes the 22.1.0 constructor slowdown for attrs classes whose generated initialization must bypass __setattr__ hooks, especially frozen or slotted classes with many assigned attributes, without changing the instances produced or their hash-related behavior.

expectation.grounded: Generated __init__ methods for @attr.s and @attr.define classes that require cached object.__setattr__ access should perform initialization through a cached bound setter so repeated field writes avoid extra lookup overhead. The same optimized assignment path should continue to be used when initializing cached hash state for affected frozen slotted classes with cache_hash, while preserving existing on_setattr bypass semantics and constructor-visible results.
expectation.conceptual: Construction of affected attrs classes should be faster in 22.2.0, particularly for classes with more initialized attributes, while producing the same field values, immutability behavior, and hashability semantics that users already rely on.

constraints.grounded: Do not change which class configurations use direct assignment versus object.__setattr__-based assignment during generated initialization. Classes that do not need cached __setattr__ handling should keep their existing constructor behavior, and classes using frozen, slots, on_setattr, or cache_hash should preserve prior observable initialization semantics apart from performance.
constraints.conceptual: This upgrade must behave as a non-regression in functionality: constructor signatures, resulting attribute values, mutation rules, and hash behavior should stay the same, with only the execution cost improving for affected classes.

behavior: When generated initialization needs to bypass __setattr__, attrs 22.2.0 should reuse a single cached bound setter for all assignments performed during that constructor call.
Construction cost for affected classes should no longer scale worse in 22.1.0 as additional attributes are initialized.
Class configurations that do not require cached __setattr__ handling should continue to use their existing initialization path without behavioral change.

If cache_hash is enabled on an affected frozen slotted class, constructor-time hash cache initialization should continue to succeed through the same bypass mechanism without changing observable hash behavior.
acceptance_criteria: When constructing an affected attrs class after upgrading to 22.2.0, initialization should be measurably faster than in 22.1.0 for classes with multiple assigned attributes, with no added per-attribute slowdown.

When constructing frozen or slotted attrs classes whose initialization bypasses __setattr__, the resulting instances should expose the same initialized field values and immutability behavior as before the upgrade.
When cache_hash is enabled for an affected class, constructing an instance should still leave it hashable with unchanged observable hash semantics.
When a class configuration does not require cached object.__setattr__ handling, its constructor behavior should remain unchanged by the upgrade.

task_8.title: Type narrowing for attrs.has()
task_8.description: Version 22.2.0 improves the typing contract of attrs class detection by making attrs.has() and attr.has() act as type guards for AttrsInstance on supported Python versions. This helps static type checkers understand that a value has attrs-generated attributes after a successful has() check, without changing runtime behavior.

synthesized_requirement.problem_statement: Ensure that upgrading to 22.2.0 provides improved static typing for attrs class detection so that a positive attrs.has() or attr.has() check is recognized by type checkers as proof that the checked value is an attrs instance.

expectation.grounded: On Python 3.10 and newer, attrs.has() and attr.has() should be typed as TypeGuard[AttrsInstance], allowing type checkers to narrow the checked object to AttrsInstance within the true branch of the condition. The public callable names remain attrs.has() and attr.has(), and their typing improvement should expose attrs-specific members consistent with AttrsInstance after a successful check.
expectation.conceptual: When application code checks an object with attrs.has() or attr.has() and the result is true, static analysis tools should understand that the object is an attrs-defined instance and permit attrs-instance attribute access accordingly.

constraints.grounded: This upgrade should preserve the existing public API and runtime semantics of attrs.has() and attr.has(); the observable change is limited to static type information. The narrowing guarantee applies only where TypeGuard support is available, and unsuccessful checks must not narrow the value to AttrsInstance.
constraints.conceptual: The change should improve developer typing feedback without altering how the library behaves at runtime. It should only strengthen type inference in environments that support the newer typing feature and should not misclassify objects when the check is false.

behavior: attrs.has() is recognized by type checkers as a type guard for AttrsInstance on supported Python versions.
attr.has() is recognized by type checkers as a type guard for AttrsInstance on supported Python versions.
Inside a branch guarded by a true attrs.has() or attr.has() result, the checked value is narrowed to an attrs instance type for static analysis.
No runtime behavior change is introduced for attrs.has() or attr.has(); the update affects typing metadata only.
acceptance_criteria: When code checks a value with attrs.has() and the condition is true, static type checking should treat that value as an AttrsInstance within that branch.
When code checks a value with attr.has() and the condition is true, static type checking should treat that value as an AttrsInstance within that branch.
When the check result is false, the value should not be narrowed to an attrs instance type.
Upgrading to 22.2.0 should not change the runtime return behavior or public callable surface of attrs.has() or attr.has().

task_9.title: Expose AttrsInstance at Runtime for Pyright Compatibility
task_9.description: The upgrade makes `AttrsInstance` a real runtime export from both `attr` and `attrs` so applications can reference it directly in annotations and runtime introspection without missing-symbol issues, improving compatibility with Pyright and similar tooling.

synthesized_requirement.problem_statement: Ensure that `AttrsInstance` is available as a public runtime type in both `attr` and `attrs`, so users can reference it consistently in application code and type annotations without tool-specific type errors or missing runtime symbols.

expectation.grounded: The library should define `attr.AttrsInstance` as a runtime-accessible public type and re-export it as `attrs.AttrsInstance`. Both modules should expose `AttrsInstance` through their public API surface so consumers can import or reference it directly, and static analysis tools such as Pyright can resolve `attrs.AttrsInstance` as an actual runtime type rather than a stub-only name.
expectation.conceptual: Users should be able to use `AttrsInstance` from either public namespace as a normal exported type. Referencing that type in annotations or runtime-aware tooling should work consistently instead of failing because the symbol only existed in typing metadata.

constraints.grounded: This change should remain limited to public availability of `AttrsInstance` in `attr` and `attrs`. Existing exported APIs must remain intact, and the upgrade should not alter unrelated attrs behaviors beyond making `AttrsInstance` resolvable and publicly visible at runtime.
constraints.conceptual: The upgrade should add missing type availability without changing unrelated library behavior. Existing consumer code should continue to work, with the only observable difference being that the previously missing public type can now be resolved normally.

behavior: `attr.AttrsInstance` exists as a runtime type.
`attrs.AttrsInstance` is publicly re-exported and resolves to the same public type contract.
`AttrsInstance` appears in the public export surface of both `attr` and `attrs`.
Code that references `attrs.AttrsInstance` in type annotations or runtime inspection no longer depends on stub-only availability.
Type checkers that require a runtime-visible symbol, including Pyright, can recognize `attrs.AttrsInstance` without reporting missing-type usage caused by the library export.
acceptance_criteria: When a user imports `AttrsInstance` from `attr`, the import should succeed and return a public runtime type.
When a user accesses `attrs.AttrsInstance`, the symbol should be present and usable as a public type.
When application code annotates values with `attrs.AttrsInstance`, the annotation should reference a real exported library symbol rather than a stub-only placeholder.
When tools or user code inspect the public exports of `attr` or `attrs`, `AttrsInstance` should be included.
When upgrading from 22.1.0 to 22.2.0, the observable change should be improved availability and compatibility of `AttrsInstance` without unrelated API regressions.

task_7.title: Improve attrs class creation performance
task_7.description: attrs 22.2.0 reduces overhead in dynamic code generation for attrs classes by replacing performance-sensitive template formatting with f-strings. The upgrade is intended to deliver about a 5% class-creation improvement, including for simple classes, without changing the public behavior of generated constructors, representations, comparisons, or hashes.

synthesized_requirement.problem_statement: Ensure that upgrading to attrs 22.2.0 preserves the observable behavior of attrs-generated classes while delivering the documented class-creation performance improvement, including for simple classes and for generated initialization, representation, comparison, and hashing behavior.

expectation.grounded: Creating classes through attrs should be measurably faster in 22.2.0 because performance-sensitive generated code is now assembled with f-string-based templates. The public behavior of generated `__init__`, `__repr__`, equality/comparison methods, and hash methods should remain stable: defaults, factories, converters, validators, `eq_key`, `cache_hash`, exception initialization, and custom `repr` callables must continue to produce the same observable results.
expectation.conceptual: The upgrade should improve attrs class creation speed without changing how attrs-decorated classes behave. Existing application code should keep seeing the same constructor behavior, object representations, comparisons, and hashing semantics, but with lower overhead when attrs builds those classes.

constraints.grounded: Do not introduce new required public inputs or alter the observable outputs of generated attrs methods. Recursive `__repr__` handling must continue to short-circuit repeated self-reference, fields excluded from `repr` must remain omitted, and configured custom repr, equality-key, validator, converter, default, factory, and hash-cache behaviors must remain intact.
constraints.conceptual: Treat this as a non-breaking performance upgrade. All existing attrs field options and generated-method edge cases should continue to work the same way from a user perspective.

behavior: Attrs class creation and related code-generation paths are optimized to reduce overhead, with the release note indicating roughly a 5% improvement even for simple classes.

Generated `__repr__` continues to produce a class-qualified representation that includes only repr-enabled fields, applies custom repr callables when configured, and returns an abbreviated recursive marker instead of recursing indefinitely.
Generated equality, ordering, and hash methods continue to use configured field values and `eq_key` or hash-caching behavior without changing their observable results.

Generated `__init__` continues to honor defaults, factories, converters, validators, keyword-only handling, slot versus dict assignment, and exception-style base initialization while benefiting from the lower template-generation overhead.
acceptance_criteria: When defining attrs classes after the upgrade, class creation should be faster than before, including for simple classes, without requiring application code changes.
When an attrs class relies on a generated `__init__`, it should continue to accept the same inputs and apply defaults, factories, converters, validators, and exception initialization as before.

When calling `repr()` on an attrs instance, it should continue to include only repr-enabled fields, use any configured custom repr formatting, and avoid infinite recursion by abbreviating repeated self-reference.
When comparing or hashing attrs instances, results should remain consistent with the previously configured comparison, `eq_key`, ordering, and hash-caching semantics.

task_11.title: Harden attrs pickling against class attribute changes
task_11.description: Upgrading from attrs 22.1.0 to 22.2.0 makes generated pickling more robust when an attrs class changes after objects were serialized. Serialized state is matched by attribute name instead of positional order so older pickles can be restored without shifting values onto the wrong fields when attributes are added, removed, or reordered.

synthesized_requirement.problem_statement: Ensure that pickled attrs-based objects can be unpickled safely even if the current class definition no longer exactly matches the version that produced the pickle, without misassigning persisted values to the wrong attributes.

expectation.grounded: Generated attrs pickling support should expose state through `__getstate__` and restore it through `__setstate__` using attribute-name mappings rather than positional tuples. During unpickling, only attributes whose names exist in both the serialized state and the current attrs class should be assigned; attributes missing from either side should be skipped instead of being matched positionally.
expectation.conceptual: Pickle compatibility for attrs classes should be resilient to schema evolution. Restoring an older serialized object should keep matching fields intact, ignore fields that no longer exist, and avoid placing old data into newly added or differently ordered fields.

constraints.grounded: Do not regress normal restoration for unchanged attrs classes. Do not assign serialized values to a different attribute solely because of ordering, do not restore removed attributes onto the current object, and do not synthesize values for attributes that were not present in the serialized state.
constraints.conceptual: The upgrade must preserve existing pickle behavior for unchanged models while preventing data corruption when a class evolves. Missing fields should be ignored, and new fields should not be populated with unrelated legacy values.

behavior: Generated attrs pickling state is represented by attribute name rather than by attribute position.
Unpickling restores each saved value only to the current attribute with the same name.
If a previously serialized attribute no longer exists on the current attrs class, unpickling skips that state entry instead of assigning it elsewhere.
If the current attrs class has additional attributes that were not serialized, unpickling leaves those attributes untouched rather than consuming an old positional value.
Reordering attributes across class versions does not change which saved value maps to which attribute during unpickling.
acceptance_criteria: When an attrs object is pickled and unpickled against an unchanged class definition, it should restore the original values for the same attributes.

When an object was pickled from an older attrs class version and the current version has removed one of those attributes, unpickling should restore the remaining shared attributes and ignore the removed field.

When an object was pickled from an older attrs class version and the current version has added a new attribute, unpickling should restore only the previously serialized matching attributes and should not assign an old value to the new attribute.
When the order of attributes differs between the serialized class version and the current attrs class version, unpickling should still restore values to the correct attribute names.

task_10.title: Correct ABC abstractness for dict-backed attrs classes
task_10.description: Upgrading to 22.2.0 changes how attrs finalizes non-slotted classes on Python 3.10 and later so abstract base class status is recalculated after attrs finishes building the class. This fixes incorrect abstractness detection for dict-backed attrs classes and makes abstractness-dependent runtime behavior match the class's final method set.

synthesized_requirement.problem_statement: Ensure that on Python 3.10 and later, dict-backed attrs classes correctly reflect abstract base class status after attrs finishes building the class, so classes that satisfy inherited abstract methods become usable and classes with missing abstract methods remain abstract.

expectation.grounded: For attrs classes built as dict classes, class finalization on Python 3.10 and later should refresh ABC metadata using abc.update_abstractmethods(). After decoration, abstractness checks on the resulting class should align with the final public method set: a class that now implements inherited abstract methods should no longer be treated as abstract, while a class that still lacks required abstract methods should remain abstract.
expectation.conceptual: After upgrading, attrs classes should report abstract or concrete status based on the methods they actually expose once attrs has finished constructing the class. Users should be able to instantiate classes that have become concrete, and still be prevented from instantiating classes that remain abstract.

constraints.grounded: This change is limited to Python 3.10 and later and applies to attrs dict-class construction behavior. It should not change the observable behavior of unaffected Python versions, and it should not expand this abstractness refresh beyond the dict-class construction path covered by the update.
constraints.conceptual: Only the correctness of abstractness detection should change. Existing class-construction behavior outside the affected runtime and class style should remain stable.

behavior: On Python 3.10 and later, attrs recalculates abstract-method status after finalizing a dict-backed class.
If attrs-generated or attrs-patched methods satisfy inherited abstract-method requirements, the resulting class becomes observable as concrete.
If inherited abstract methods are still missing after class construction, the resulting class remains observable as abstract.

Runtime behavior that depends on whether an affected attrs class is abstract should reflect the class's final method set rather than stale abstractness metadata from before attrs finished building the class.
acceptance_criteria: When a dict-backed attrs class on Python 3.10 or later ends up providing all inherited abstract methods after decoration, it should no longer be considered abstract.
When a dict-backed attrs class on Python 3.10 or later still omits one or more inherited abstract methods after decoration, it should still be considered abstract.
When abstractness-dependent runtime behavior is exercised for an affected attrs class, it should match the class's final post-decoration method set.

task_12.title: Add inverse validator composition with attrs.validators.not_
task_12.description: Version 22.2.0 adds a new public validator, `attrs.validators.not_`, so applications can express negative validation rules by wrapping an existing validator instead of needing separate inverted validators. The new behavior defines how wrapped validation failures are treated as success, how success is turned into a validation error, and how custom captured exception types and messages affect observable runtime behavior.

synthesized_requirement.problem_statement: Ensure that the library supports composing negative validation rules through a public `attrs.validators.not_` validator so users can declare that a value must fail another validator, with configurable captured exception types and a customizable failure message.

expectation.grounded: Expose `attrs.validators.not_(validator, *, msg=None, exc_types=(ValueError, TypeError))` as a public validator factory. The returned validator must call the wrapped validator and treat a raised exception from `exc_types` as a successful negated validation. If the wrapped validator completes without raising one of the captured exception types, the negated validator must raise `ValueError`. If `msg` is provided, it must be used for that `ValueError`; otherwise a default message is used. `exc_types` may be supplied as a single exception class or an iterable of exception classes, and invalid non-`Exception` members must be rejected during validator construction.
expectation.conceptual: Users should be able to express rules such as 'value must not satisfy this validator' by wrapping an existing validator with `attrs.validators.not_`. Validation should pass when the wrapped rule rejects the value with one of the configured exception types, fail when the wrapped rule accepts the value, allow the caller to customize the failure message, and reject invalid exception-type configuration.

constraints.grounded: Only exceptions matching `exc_types` are inverted into success. Exceptions from the wrapped validator that do not match `exc_types` must propagate unchanged. The negated validator must raise `ValueError` when the wrapped validator succeeds, and the `exc_types` configuration must contain subclasses of `Exception`.
constraints.conceptual: Negation must not hide unrelated validator failures or change behavior outside the configured exception types. It should only flip the success condition of the wrapped validator and should fail fast if its exception capture configuration is invalid.

behavior: `attrs.validators.not_` is available as a public validator for composing inverse validation rules.
By default, the negated validator treats `ValueError` and `TypeError` raised by the wrapped validator as a successful validation outcome.
If the wrapped validator accepts the value without raising a captured exception, the negated validator raises `ValueError` to indicate that the negated rule failed.
A caller may override which exception type or types count as an inverted success by supplying `exc_types`.
If the wrapped validator raises an exception outside the configured `exc_types`, that exception is not suppressed by `not_` and remains observable to the caller.
If a custom `msg` is supplied, it becomes the user-visible message for the `ValueError` raised when the wrapped validator unexpectedly succeeds.
Constructing `not_` with invalid `exc_types` members that are not subclasses of `Exception` fails immediately with a type validation error.
acceptance_criteria: When a field uses `attrs.validators.not_(wrapped_validator)` and `wrapped_validator` rejects the value by raising `ValueError` or `TypeError`, the field validation should succeed.
When a field uses `attrs.validators.not_(wrapped_validator)` and `wrapped_validator` accepts the value, validation should fail with `ValueError` from the negated validator.
When `exc_types` is set to a custom exception class or tuple of exception classes, only those exception types should count as a successful negated validation.
When the wrapped validator raises an exception that is not included in `exc_types`, that exception should be surfaced instead of being converted into a negated success.
When `msg` is provided to `attrs.validators.not_` and the wrapped validator accepts the value, the resulting `ValueError` should use the custom message.
When `exc_types` contains a value that is not an `Exception` subclass, creating the negated validator should fail rather than producing a validator with undefined behavior.

task_14.title: Add PEP 681-compatible unsafe_hash support to attrs decorators
task_14.description: The 22.2.0 update expands the attrs decorator API to accept the dataclass-style `unsafe_hash` keyword alongside `hash`. This makes `attr.s()` and `attrs.define()` compatible with PEP 681-style callers, and `unsafe_hash` becomes the effective hash setting when both keywords are provided.

synthesized_requirement.problem_statement: Ensure that supported attrs class decorators accept the dataclass-style `unsafe_hash` option so callers upgrading to 22.2.0 can control generated hashing behavior through the PEP 681-compatible keyword, with consistent results when both `unsafe_hash` and `hash` are present.

expectation.grounded: `attr.s()` and `attrs.define()` should accept an `unsafe_hash` keyword argument in addition to `hash`. `unsafe_hash=True` should produce the same hash-generation behavior as `hash=True`, `unsafe_hash=False` should behave like `hash=False`, and when `unsafe_hash` is not `None` it should override any `hash` value supplied in the same decorator call. When `unsafe_hash` is omitted, existing `hash` and automatic hash-detection behavior should remain in effect.
expectation.conceptual: Users should be able to use the standard `unsafe_hash` keyword on supported attrs decorators to opt classes into or out of generated hashing without changing the existing meaning of `hash`. If both keywords are supplied, the explicit `unsafe_hash` choice should win.

constraints.grounded: Existing callers that only use `hash` must keep their current behavior. Automatic handling for classes that rely on default hash detection must remain unchanged when `unsafe_hash` is not provided. Invalid explicit hash-control values must continue to be rejected with the same observable error type.
constraints.conceptual: The upgrade should be additive and non-breaking for existing decorator usage. It must preserve prior hashing behavior unless a caller deliberately uses the new keyword, and it must not silently accept unsupported hash settings.

behavior: `attr.s()` accepts `unsafe_hash` as a public keyword argument.
`attrs.define()` accepts `unsafe_hash` as a public keyword argument.
Providing `unsafe_hash=True` requests generated hash behavior equivalent to enabling `hash=True`.
Providing `unsafe_hash=False` requests the same non-hash-generating behavior as `hash=False`.
If both `unsafe_hash` and `hash` are provided, `unsafe_hash` determines the effective hash policy.
If `unsafe_hash` is omitted, existing `hash` handling and default hash auto-detection continue unchanged.
Unsupported explicit hash-control values continue to fail with `TypeError`.
acceptance_criteria: When a class is decorated with `attr.s(unsafe_hash=True)`, instances should be hashable under the same contract as `attr.s(hash=True)`.
When a class is decorated with `attrs.define(unsafe_hash=True)`, the decorator should accept the keyword and apply the same hash-generation behavior as `hash=True`.
When `unsafe_hash=False` is supplied to a supported decorator, it should disable generated hashing the same way `hash=False` does.
When both `hash` and `unsafe_hash` are supplied to a supported decorator, the runtime behavior should follow the `unsafe_hash` value rather than the `hash` value.
When `unsafe_hash` is not supplied, upgrading to 22.2.0 should not change the observable hashing behavior of existing decorator calls that rely on `hash` or default behavior.
When an unsupported explicit hash-control value is passed through the effective hash-setting keyword, the decorator should still raise `TypeError`.

task_13.title: Align attrs.cmp_using() type stubs with runtime defaults
task_13.description: Version 22.2.0 updates the published type information for attrs.cmp_using() so its optional comparator arguments and options are represented with default values, matching the existing runtime callable. This removes false-positive static typing friction for callers that provide only the comparison hooks or options they actually need.

synthesized_requirement.problem_statement: Ensure that typed consumers can call `attrs.cmp_using()` without being forced to supply every optional comparator and configuration argument when they only need a subset of the API.

expectation.grounded: `attrs.cmp_using()` should expose defaulted optional parameters in its distributed type stubs for `eq`, `lt`, `le`, `gt`, `ge`, `require_same_type`, and `class_name`, matching the callable's existing runtime signature. Typed calls that pass only selected comparators or options should be accepted without requiring placeholder values for omitted arguments.
expectation.conceptual: `attrs.cmp_using()` should type-check the same way it behaves at runtime: callers may specify only the comparison functions and options they need, and omitted settings should be treated as optional defaults rather than required inputs.

constraints.grounded: Do not change the runtime behavior or return contract of `attrs.cmp_using()`. The update should only correct the published typing surface so existing comparison semantics, default option behavior, and runtime validation rules remain unchanged.
constraints.conceptual: This upgrade should remove typing-only friction without altering how generated comparison helpers behave in production.

behavior: The published type signature for `attrs.cmp_using()` now marks all comparator callback parameters and option parameters as having defaults instead of requiring every argument positionally or by keyword.

Typed code may call `attrs.cmp_using()` with only `eq`, only a subset of ordering callbacks, or only selected options such as `require_same_type` and `class_name` without supplying unrelated placeholder arguments solely to satisfy the stub.

The function continues to return the same generated comparison helper type at runtime; the observable change is acceptance by static type checkers and signature-aware tooling for calls that already worked at runtime.
acceptance_criteria: When a typed project calls `attrs.cmp_using(eq=...)` and omits the other parameters, it should be accepted by the library's distributed type information.

When a typed project calls `attrs.cmp_using(eq=..., class_name=...)` or `attrs.cmp_using(eq=..., require_same_type=False)` and omits unrelated parameters, it should be accepted without requiring explicit `None` placeholders for the omitted callbacks.
When callers continue using `attrs.cmp_using()` at runtime, the generated comparison behavior and existing validation semantics should remain unchanged by this upgrade.
